How Image Generation Works

You ask for a picture of a crocodile driving a Hilux, and thirty seconds later there it is. Where did it come from? Not from a folder. Not from the internet. This is the story of how a machine paints something nobody has ever seen.

Myth to retire: "it finds a picture and hands it over"

Eight short steps. Click anywhere, tap, or use the arrow keys to move through.

Start small: a cell that goes ping

A brain cell, or the artificial kind in this machine, mostly just sits there. Sometimes it goes ping. It decides to ping based on how many pings are arriving from the cells connected to it, and how strong each connection is. That is the whole component. Everything else is just lots of them.

Click the small cells to make them ping. The thick wire counts double, because that connection is strong.

arriving: 0 · needs 3 to fire

A cell never sees the whole picture. It only ever asks one tiny question: are my neighbours pinging hard enough?

Stack them up: edges, then beak, then bird

How do you recognise a bird? You do not write rules for "bird". You build upward, layer by layer, each layer pinging when the layer below gives it something to ping about.

Bottom layer: pixels
A pixel is one tiny dot of the picture. Some bright, some dark. That is all this layer knows.
Next: edge detectors
A cell here pings when bright pixels sit beside dark ones. Bright against dark is an edge.
Next: little parts
Cells that ping when a few edges line up: a pointy thing that might be a beak, a small circle that might be an eye.
Next: a possible head
One cell pings only when a possible beak and a possible eye sit in the right place together.
Top: bird
Head plus wing plus feet, all pinging at once. A cell up here says: probably a bird.

Nobody sets those connections by hand

The connection strengths start out random. You show the machine a labelled picture and ask: bird or not? Then you nudge every connection a tiny bit in whichever direction makes the guess less wrong, and you do that across millions of labelled pictures, millions of times. That nudging is the learning. That is all "training" is.

LABEL: BIRD

The machine's guess: 50% bird, which is a coin flip. It has no idea.

labelled pictures seen: 0 · connections: random

No rules were typed in. The idea of "beak" was never programmed. It grew, because having a beak detector made the guesses less wrong.

What "labelled pictures" actually look like

This is not a mystery ingredient. A labelled dataset is just pictures with a word attached to each one. A famous one, CIFAR-10, holds 60,000 tiny photos in ten classes: cat, dog, bird, automobile, truck and so on. Sixty thousand tiny flash cards.

cat
dog
bird
automobile
truck

The real thing, browsable online: the CIFAR-10 dataset at huggingface.co/datasets/uoft-cs/cifar10. The truck and automobile classes are our stand-in for the Hilux.

Teach a machine cat versus dog from labelled examples and you can teach it any difference the same way. You just need the flash cards.

Fine differences, learnt the same way

Here in the Territory we know the difference at a glance. A machine could learn it too, from enough labelled photos, even though nobody would ever type the rules in. Click each feature to see what the layers would quietly discover.

Crocodile
Alligator

Three tells, all learnable from examples.

There is no famous crocodile-versus-alligator dataset. But you can picture building one: a few thousand labelled photos of each, and the machine would find the snout, the teeth and the colour on its own. That is worth sitting with.

Now run the whole thing in reverse

After all that training, the machine holds a rich sense of what things look like: the ridged back of a crocodile, the metal shine of a car door. Generation uses that sense backwards. Start with a square of pure random static, like an old TV between channels. Then ask: if this static were slowly becoming "a crocodile driving a Hilux", which speckles should change, and which way? Nudge them. Look again. Nudge again.

Honest version of the fancy word: the machine is removing noise a little at a time until a picture that matches your words is left standing.

Why everyone's crocodile is different

The static it starts from is fresh and random every single time. Different static means the nudges land differently, so the same words end somewhere new. Same prompt, three runs:

Generative AI is not looking anything up. It is imagining, from noise, guided by your words. That is why no two are alike.

Now prove it with the room

Everyone, at the same time, give your AI tool the exact same prompt:

Show me a picture of a crocodile driving a Hilux.

Then compare screens. Thirty people, thirty different crocodiles. You now know exactly why: thirty squares of fresh static, each nudged until it matched the same nine words.

The one idea to keep

The machine learnt what things look like from millions of labelled pictures, feature by feature. To make a new picture, it runs that understanding in reverse, starting from random static. Fresh static every time is why the same words never paint the same picture twice.

Where this connects

This deck's sibling, How AI Predicts the Next Word, tells the same story for text: weighted dice instead of nudged static, and the same lesson at the end. The machine predicts; it does not look up.
